title: Expressing Time, Place and Cause
keyIdea: Small joining words tell the reader when, where and why. Conjunctions like when, before, after and while show time; because and so show cause. Adverbs like first, next, soon and therefore link one sentence to the next. Prepositions start phrases like during the lesson (when), under the bridge (where) and because of the rain (why).

kid: Some words tell us when. Before, after, while and when are time words. 'Wash your hands before you eat.'
Some words tell us why. Because gives the reason. So gives what happened next. 'It was cold, so I wore a hat.' 'I wore a hat because it was cold.'
Take care. Swap because and so, and the sentence goes back to front. 'It was cold because I wore a hat' is silly!

Do not start each sentence with then. Use first, next, after that and finally. They help the reader follow the order. Short phrases can say when, where or why too: during the film, under the bed, because of the rain.
adult: In the English national curriculum, Year 3 pupils learn to express time, place and cause using conjunctions (when, before, after, while, so, because), adverbs (then, next, soon, therefore) and prepositions (before, after, during, in, because of). The grammar terms they meet are conjunction, clause, subordinate clause, adverb and preposition.

A conjunction such as because or after joins a main clause to a subordinate clause: 'We went inside because it was raining.' A time adverb links ideas across sentences: 'First, she opened the door. Then, she stepped outside.' A preposition starts a phrase: 'during the lesson', 'behind the shed', 'because of the noise'.

The commonest slip is swapping because and so. 'Because' comes before the cause; 'so' comes before the result, so swapping them reverses the meaning. Another is a 'then, then, then' story where every sentence starts the same way. A third is muddling before and after, which flips the order of events.

When a subordinate clause moves to the front ('After the bell rang, we lined up'), a comma marks where it ends. Pupils often put it in the wrong place. The lab practises each idea: joining clauses, ordering a story with time adverbs, sorting phrases into when, where and why, building cause-and-result sentences, and placing the comma.

familyTip: At bedtime, retell the day using first, next, after that and finally. Then play 'because or so': say half a sentence like 'I was hungry…' and take turns finishing it with 'so…' and then with 'because…'.

visual.caption: Does the bold word show time or cause? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: We lined up after the bell rang.
Wash your hands before you eat.
I wore a coat because it was cold.
It rained, so the match stopped.
We stayed in because of the storm.
He forgot his key. Therefore, he knocked.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: join clauses with conjunctions, fix a 'then, then' story, sort when, where and why phrases, and place a fronted clause's comma.

practice.prompt: Which word fits? 'The pond froze ___ it was so cold.'
practice.hint: The cold is the reason. Which word comes before a reason?
practice.explain: Because. The cold is the cause, and 'because' comes in front of the cause.

practice.prompt: Mia waited {n} minutes. The bus was late. Which sentence joins these the right way?
choices: Mia waited {n} minutes because the bus was late.
Mia waited {n} minutes so the bus was late.
The bus was late because Mia waited {n} minutes.
practice.hint: What is the reason Mia waited? Put 'because' in front of the reason.
practice.explain: The late bus is the cause, so it goes after 'because': Mia waited {n} minutes because the bus was late.

practice.hint: Time phrases often start with during, before, after or on.
practice.explain: During the match tells when. Under the table tells where, and because of the wind tells why.

practice.prompt: The cake baked for {n} minutes. Then we ate it. Which word fits? '___ the cake had baked for {n} minutes, we ate it.'
practice.hint: Which came first, the baking or the eating?
practice.explain: After. The baking came first, so 'After the cake had baked for {n} minutes, we ate it.'

pool.explain: Because gives a reason. While and after are time conjunctions.

pool.prompt: 'Ben was tired, ___ he went to bed early.' Which word fits?
pool.hint: Being tired came first. Going to bed is what happened as a result.
pool.explain: So. 'So' comes in front of the result. 'Because' would mean going to bed made Ben tired.

pool.prompt: Which is the best start for the last sentence of a story?
pool.hint: Which time adverb means the very last thing?
pool.explain: Finally means the last thing. First opens a story, and next moves it on.

pool.prompt: Which sentence has the comma in the right place?
choices: After the film ended, we went home.
After the film, ended we went home.
After, the film ended we went home.
pool.hint: The comma goes at the end of the fronted clause.
pool.explain: 'After the film ended, we went home.' The comma marks where the fronted clause stops.

pool.prompt: Sam read {n} pages while he waited. What does 'while' tell us?
choices: He read and waited at the same time
pool.hint: While is a time word. Does it mean before, after or at the same time?
pool.explain: While means at the same time. Sam read {n} pages during the wait.

pool.prompt: The match was stopped after {n} minutes because of the snow. What does 'because of the snow' tell us?
pool.hint: Because of starts a phrase that gives a reason.
pool.explain: Why. 'Because of the snow' is the cause. 'After {n} minutes' is the phrase that tells when.

pool.prompt: 'Ali packed his bag ___ he left for school.' Which word fits?
pool.hint: He needs his bag at school. Which happened first?
pool.explain: Before. Packing came first. 'After' would mean he packed once he had already gone.
